 Warriors feel ‘sting' in familiar way with wasted opportunity vs. Grizzlies 
 The Golden State Warriors' loss to the Memphis Grizzlies on Friday was reminiscent of the "clutch games" they dropped early last season. 
 By Monte Poole, Warriors Insider • 
 Published October 24, 2026 • 
 Updated on October 24, 2026 at 12:03 am 
 BOOKMARKER 
 Share 
 NBC Universal, Inc. 
 Warriors star Steph Curry speaks to reporters after Golden State’s 111-108 loss in its home opener Friday to the Memphis Grizzlies at Chase Center. 
 SAN FRANCISCO – Sitting at the podium during his pregame news conference Friday afternoon, coach Steve Kerr explained that was “preaching” to the Warriors. His word, not mine.
 He was emphasizing the factors that will dictate the fate of Golden State’s season, the key phrase being “winning on the margins.” Basketball-speak for playing smart and hard, all the way to the buzzer.
 The Warriors failed that test in the first half of their home opener, falling behind by as much as 13 points. They aced it in the third quarter and in the first eight-plus minutes of the fourth, building a 12-point lead.

 They absolutely torched it over the final 3:34, slinking off the Chase Center floor with a 111-108 loss to the Memphis Grizzlies.
 “There's losses,” Stephen Curry said, “and there's ways that you lose, like tonight, that kind of sting a little bit more.”
 This performance was reminiscent of some of the “clutch games” Golden State lost early last season that kept it handcuffed to mediocrity. Earn a decent lead and then, with the smell of victory entering their nostrils, do enough wretched stuff to give it away.
 After the Warriors went up 106-94 on a De’Anthony Melton triple with 3:47 remaining, they fed Memphis a 17-0 run that had them trailing by five (111-106) with 10.2 seconds remaining. The Warriors were stunned, the sellout crowd (18,064) stupefied.

 The Grizzlies during that stretch benefitted from shooting 4 of 7 from the field, including a couple 3-pointers, as well as going 7 of 8 from the line while Golden State was missing eight consecutive shots and committing two turnovers.
 “Pretty much everything went wrong,” Curry said. “It's a tough pill to swallow, considering we played really solidly, especially in that second half, to give ourselves a lead and be in control of the game for as long as we did. It's a tough one.”
 The loss dropped the Warriors to 0-2 in a 2026-27 NBA season they know they’ll have to be superb simply to be relevant in the Western Conference. For a while, they not only seemed to understand the assignment but began applying it.
 The Warriors overcame a first half during which they were outshot (53.5 percent to 40.5), out-rebounded (24-17), outscored in transition points (13-0) and gave the Grizzlies 20 points off 11 turnovers. They were getting clobbered on the margins and the metrics.
 They turned things around in the third quarter, winning on field-goal percentage, rebounds and forcing six Memphis turnovers while committing only three. The considerably smaller Warriors even posted an advantage in paint points. From the beginning of third quarter through Melton’s triple, they outscored the Grizzlies by 16 (50-34).
 “The effort, the energy was all there, so it's a shame that we didn't close the game because I thought the guys all game long competed,” Kerr said. “But we didn't deserve to win the game because we didn't make the plays that we needed to at the end.”
 Golden State pulled ahead by practicing what the coaching staff is preaching. Each man on the roster understands on most nights they will operate at a size disadvantage, and some nights there will be a visible talent disadvantage.
 Memphis is bigger, but not necessarily more talented – which is why this was such a lost opportunity.
 “Everybody says there's another game tomorrow,” Curry said. “But the idea of how important every game is for us to build the right habits, the right execution mentality to try to win. And the fact that you gave one away like this . . . you might lose a little sleep over it tonight, but try to bounce back tomorrow.”
 Preach. Keep preaching. Twenty good minutes are never enough – especially if they don’t include the last four of a close game.
